# DRUG ALLERGIES

# Importance of history

The nature and circumstances of a possible previous reaction including the timing should be considered. In many cases, previous reactions are clearly not due to drug allergy.

# Types of reactions

*Immediate - within one hour of starting drug administration.

Type I reactions present with urticaria, hypotension, angioedema, bronchospasm, or anaphylaxis and occur within an hour of exposure. These reactions are immunoglobulin E (IgE) and mast cell and/or basophil mediated.

*Delayed - After one hour of starting administration (usually after 6 days)

1) Type II reactions manifest as hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and neutropenia. They are caused by antibody (usually IgG)- mediated cell destruction.
2) Type III reactions can manifest as serum sickness, vasculitis or Arthus reaction, and are caused by IgG:drug immune complex deposition and complement activation.
3) Type IV reactions typically manifest as contact dermatitis, morbilliform reactions, severe exfoliative dermatoses (Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis) and other presentations. They are T-cell mediated.

Repeated exposures lead to reactions that are of the same type.

# Beta-lactam allergies

Approximately 10% of patients report a beta-lactam allergy. Up to 90% of these patients can tolerate penicillin and have been designated penicillin allergic unnecessarily. Patients allergic to cephalosporins will have a cross-reaction to penicillins 3% to 5% of the time. Overall, patients with a history of penicillin allergy can tolerate cephalosporins although there are rare reports to severe, sometimes fatal anaphylactic reactions. Neither penicillin- or cephalosporin-allergic patients will react to aztreonam. The degree of cross-reactivity of penicillins and cephalosporins with carbapenems appears to be low.

# Therapeutic implications

If a patient has had an immediate reaction to a drug in the past, an allergy specialist should evaluate the patient before a drug of the same class is administered to the patient. Patients with delayed onset reactions causing fever, systemic symptoms or mucosal involvement should also be evaluated by an allergy specialist before a drug of the same class is administered.

# Desensitization

A patient with previous Type I reaction to a beta-lactam can be desensitized and then receive therapeutic doses of the same class within a day. Severe reactions during desensitization are uncommon. Pharmacy service must be contacted for assistance and drug preparation. Infectious Disease consultation strongly recommended.
